newsitem.title: USA: Clinton unveils tax-free internet strategy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton unveils tax-free internet strategy.

text.p: Hailing the Internet as an engine for future economic growth, U.S. President Bill Clinton on Tuesday unveiled a largely laissez-faire policy to promote commerce in cyberspace unburdened by new government taxes.

"In the 21st century, we can build much of our prosperity on innovations in cyberspace in ways that most of us cannot even imagine," Clinton said at a White House ceremony to unveil a 30-page report on electronic commerce.
"Today we act to ensure that international trade on the Internet remains free of new discriminatory taxes, free of tariffs, free from burdens and regulations, and safe from piracy," Clinton added.
Like many of Clinton's second-term initiatives, the report envisages only modest government action.

The report, entitled "A Framework for Global Electronic Commerce," urges that no new taxes or tarrifs be imposed on Internet transactions. Nor should the government dictate technical standards or protocols for the network, it said.

Commerce over the Internet, which ranges from the sale of books and compact disks to gambling and live pornography, is projected to grow from less than $1 billion last year to perhaps $5 billion to $10 billion by the year 2000.
Started as a government research project in the 1960s, the computer network has only recently emerged as an important medium for commerce.

An informal consensus among university and government researchers has set policies for the network thus far, but business has challenged that approach with a host of difficult issues, including taxation and copyright protection.
Clinton, a self-described "technophobe," said the network needed a clearer set of rules but he envisaged a limited government role.
"In many ways, electronic commerce is like the Wild West for the global economy," Clinton said. "Our task is to make sure that it's safe and stable terrain for those who wish to trade on it."
Clinton said he wanted to accomplish several goals over the next 12 months, instructing top officials to:
-- work with the World Trade Organization to declare the Internet a global free-trade zone;
-- work with industry to develop technology and codes of conduct to protect individuals' privacy on the Internet;
-- encourage the development of technology, like the proposed television V-chip, to allow parents to screen their children from objectionable material on the Internet.
Companies doing business on the Internet praised the "hands off" approach as appropriate for the fast-changing medium.

"The private sector, an open market and competition -- not the government -- will regulate opportunity and the pace of innovation," International Business Machines Corp Chairman Louis Gerstner said at the ceremony.

"Inconsistent and varied policies regarding the Internet, including tax policy, could limit the ability of companies to participate in electronic commerce," added America Online President Steve Case, who also attended the ceremony.
The one area where Clinton has clearly signalled an intent to influence the medium is in preventing children from using it to get access to pornography.

The administration suffered a defeat last week when the Supreme Court struck down a law that outlawed the display of indecent images where they could be seen by children on grounds that it violated the first amendment.

"A hands-off approach to electronic commerce must not mean indifference when it comes to raising and protecting children," Clinton said, adding he will host a conference with teachers, parents and internet users to find a way to protect children from Internet.

The report advocates the use of technology, and possibly a voluntary ratings system, to help parents screen out smut. The largely laissez-faire document was prepared by Ira Magaziner, who spearheaded Clinton's failed 1994 bid for a massive overhaul of the U.S. health care system.
